title: Investigating Students’ Preferences for AI Roles in Mathematical Modelling: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence should function during mathematical modelling activities and how students’ design thinking (DT), computational thinking (CT), and mathematical modelling self-efficacy (MMSE) relate to their preferences for different AI roles. The authors address three main questions: the relationships among DT, CT, and MMSE; which AI roles students prefer during modelling; and whether preferences vary across learner profiles. The study is positioned in the context of AI-supported mathematics education, with a focus on higher-order thinking and the challenges students face in abstraction, representation, and iterative reasoning during mathematical modelling.

The intervention compared five AI roles in mathematical modelling tasks: Tutor, Teaching Assistant, Peer Student, Struggling Student, and Excellent Student, plus a no-assistance baseline. The AI responses were generated with GPT-based models using role-specific prompts. Participants completed one baseline task and five AI-supported tasks in a within-subjects, counterbalanced experiment conducted fully online. Quantitative data included pre-task surveys measuring MMSE, CT, and DT, as well as post-task ratings of confidence, helpfulness, and ease of interaction; qualitative data came from open-ended feedback about the AI roles.

The final sample included 26 university students aged 18 or older, all from non-STEM majors and without university-level mathematics coursework, chosen because the authors considered their math background comparable to that of high school graduates. The paper also frames the task design to reflect high-school-level mathematical modelling problems, but the actual participants were undergraduates. The study appears to have been conducted with students in Hong Kong SAR through The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, and all activities were completed online with short modelling tasks lasting four minutes each.

The main findings were that DT and CT were both significant positive predictors of mathematical modelling self-efficacy, with DT showing the stronger effect. Students clearly disliked the Struggling Student AI role, rating it significantly worse than Tutor, Teaching Assistant, Peer, and Excellent Student roles on preference, confidence, helpfulness, and ease of interaction. Among the four competent AI roles, there were no significant preference differences overall, suggesting that students valued competent support more than a specific pedagogical persona. A subgroup analysis found only one notable difference: students with higher design thinking scores preferred the Teaching Assistant role more than lower-DT students. The qualitative analysis reinforced these results by showing that students valued clarity, guidance, and supportive interaction, while criticizing ambiguity and poor pedagogical value.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family conversational AI used here as a role-playing chatbot that can adopt different instructional personas.
identified_tools.use_case: A GPT-based AI agent was used in five role conditions during short mathematical modelling tasks: Tutor, Teaching Assistant, Peer Student, Struggling Student, and Excellent Student. Responses were generated with GPT-based models using role-specific system prompts.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports a randomized within-subjects experiment on students’ preferences and experience with AI roles in mathematical modelling, but it does not report direct learning-performance or test-score effects by role. Instead, students significantly preferred competent roles over the Struggling Student role, with the overall Friedman test showing differences in rankings across roles, χ2(4, N = 26) = 28.83, p < .001. Tutor was ranked most favorably (M = 2.35, SD = 1.02) and Struggling Student least favorably (M = 4.42, SD = 1.17).
findings.measure: Role preference rankings in mathematical modelling support
findings.effect_size: r=0.85 Tutor vs Struggling; r=0.80 Excellent vs Struggling; r=0.67 Peer vs Struggling; r=0.57 TA vs Struggling

findings.finding_summary: AI role significantly affected students’ task confidence during mathematical modelling, χ2(4, N = 26) = 24.85, p < .001. Students reported the highest confidence with Excellent Student (M = 3.69, SD = 1.19) and Tutor (M = 3.65, SD = 1.16), while Struggling Student was lowest (M = 1.88, SD = 1.24); post hoc tests showed Struggling Student was significantly lower than Excellent (W = 28.5, p = .004), TA (W = 12.0, p = .005), and Tutor (W = 9.0, p = .001).
findings.measure: Task confidence ratings (Likert scale) after each AI-role-supported modelling task

findings.finding_summary: Perceived helpfulness differed significantly by AI role, χ2(4, N = 26) = 32.63, p < .001. Tutor was rated most helpful (M = 4.12, SD = 0.91), followed by Excellent Student (M = 3.96, SD = 1.04), while Struggling Student was lowest (M = 1.92, SD = 1.23); Struggling Student was significantly less helpful than Tutor (W = 2.5, p < .001), Excellent (W = 17.0, p = .001), Peer (W = 22.0, p = .004), and TA (W = 13.0, p = .005).

Ease of interaction also varied significantly across AI roles, χ2(4, N = 26) = 36.43, p < .001. Tutor was easiest to interact with (M = 4.08, SD = 0.93), followed by Excellent Student (M = 3.81, SD = 0.98), whereas Struggling Student was lowest (M = 1.81, SD = 1.17); Struggling Student was significantly worse than Tutor (W = 2.0, p < .001), Peer (W = 13.0, p = .001), and Excellent (W = 18.5, p = .002).

Baseline learner characteristics were associated with differences in AI role preference only in a limited way. Higher design thinking participants preferred the Teaching Assistant role more than lower design thinking participants (Mhigh = 2.38, SD = 1.04; Mlow = 3.46, SD = 1.56; p = .049), while no significant differences were found by computational thinking or mathematical modelling self-efficacy for any AI role (all ps > .188 or > .178 as reported).
findings.measure: AI role preference differences by baseline DT, CT, and MMSE groups

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical randomized within-subjects trial using counterbalancing, but the final sample is small (n=26) and the reported outcomes are mainly preferences and self-reports rather than objective achievement gains.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows statistically significant differences in perceived confidence, helpfulness, interaction ease, and role preference, but impact on actual mathematical learning performance is unclear and effect sizes are only reported for preference contrasts involving the Struggling role.
